title: Hangover Smoothie Recipes: 5 Easy Blends for the Morning After
excerpt: Five hangover smoothie recipes for nausea, thirst, fatigue, and hunger, what each ingredient can and can't do, what to skip, and when a hangover needs a doctor.
metaDescription: Five easy hangover smoothie recipes for nausea, thirst, and low energy, with what each ingredient really does, what to skip, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a hangover smoothie won't cure a hangover, but it's one of the easiest ways to get fluids, calories, potassium, and a little protein into your body when you feel too rough to eat a real meal. The best ones are cold, simple, and gentle on the stomach. Below are five recipes for different kinds of hangover (queasy, thirsty, starving, wiped out, and too hot to function), plus what each ingredient can and can't do, and when a hangover is something more serious.

**The quick rules:** start with water or coconut water as the base, add a banana or other soft fruit, add something with protein (yogurt, kefir, milk, or oats), and add a small pinch of salt if you're very thirsty. Use fresh ginger if you feel sick. Sip it slowly. Keep drinking plain water through the day as well, because one smoothie isn't enough fluid on its own.

> **When a hangover needs more than a smoothie.** Most hangovers fade within a day. **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe stomach pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, confusion, or fainting, or the symptoms are getting worse instead of better after 24 hours. If you drink heavily most days and feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or start seeing or hearing things when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, and it needs a doctor, not a home remedy. If someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has a seizure, call 911 (or your local emergency number). This article is general information, not medical advice.

## What a Hangover Smoothie Can and Can't Do

It helps to be clear about what's going on in your body the morning after, because it explains why some ingredients are worth adding and others are just marketing.

Researchers still don't fully understand what causes hangovers. The main suspects are:

- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol lowers a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. That's why you pee more when you drink, and why you wake up thirsty with a dry mouth.
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response, and studies have linked higher levels of inflammatory signaling molecules to worse hangover symptoms.
- **Acetaldehyde.** When your liver breaks down alcohol, the first by-product is acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that's normally cleared quickly but can contribute to nausea, flushing, and feeling unwell.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it breaks up deep and REM sleep later in the night.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid, which is behind the nausea and the burning feeling.
- **Low blood sugar in some people.** Alcohol interferes with the liver's ability to release glucose. This doesn't explain hangovers by itself, but it can add to shakiness, weakness, and fatigue.

A smoothie can realistically help with three of these. It replaces some fluid, it gives you easy-to-digest carbohydrates to steady your blood sugar, and if you add ginger it may calm your stomach. It also gives you calories at a time when you probably skipped dinner or ate badly.

What it **can't** do is speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol or acetaldehyde, reverse the sleep you lost, or "detox" you. There is no good evidence that any fruit, vegetable, or superfood powder does that. Be skeptical of recipes that promise to "flush toxins" or "reset your liver."

One more useful piece of context: research comparing people's blood electrolyte levels with how bad their hangover feels has generally found only a weak link. Rehydrating is still worthwhile and makes you feel better, but it isn't the whole story, which is why fluids help without fully fixing a hangover.

## The Building Blocks: What Each Ingredient Brings

Here's a quick reference for the most common hangover smoothie ingredients and what you can honestly expect from each.

| Ingredient | What it adds | Honest take |
|---|---|---|
| Banana | Potassium, soft carbs, creamy texture | Easy on the stomach and helps make the smoothie filling. Good base for most recipes. |
| Coconut water | Fluid, potassium, a little sugar | Hydrating and pleasant, but low in sodium. Add a pinch of salt if you're very thirsty. |
| Fresh ginger | Sharp, warming flavor | Has decent evidence for easing nausea in other settings, such as pregnancy and motion sickness. Worth trying if you feel sick. |
| Plain yogurt or kefir | Protein, fluid, live cultures | Steadies the smoothie and keeps you full. Choose plain to avoid a sugar crash. |
| Rolled oats | Slow carbs, fiber | Makes the smoothie more like a meal. Use a small amount if your stomach is upset. |
| Spinach | Folate, magnesium, potassium | Mild flavor in a fruit smoothie. Fine in small handfuls; skip if very nauseous. |
| Berries | Vitamin C, fiber, color | Good flavor and nutrients. No good evidence they reduce hangover symptoms directly. |
| Watermelon | Mostly water, a little potassium | Very hydrating and refreshing. Low in protein, so pair with yogurt if you're hungry. |
| Honey | Simple sugars | Small amounts help if your blood sugar feels low. Not a cure. |
| Pinch of salt | Sodium | Helps your body hold on to the fluid you drink. A small pinch is enough. |
| Orange or pineapple juice | Sugar, vitamin C, flavor | Fine in small splashes. Acidic juices can irritate a sore stomach. |

If you want more detail on single ingredients, we've looked at [bananas for a hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover), [coconut water](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover), and [ginger](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) in their own guides.

## Recipe 1: Banana-Ginger Stomach Settler (Best for Nausea)

This is the one to make if you wake up queasy and the thought of food makes things worse. It's mild, cold, and gentle, and the ginger is the key ingredient.

**Ingredients (makes 1 large glass):**

- 1 ripe banana (frozen if you have one)
- 1 thumb-sized piece of fresh ginger, peeled (about 1 teaspoon grated), or 1/4 teaspoon ground ginger
- 1/2 cup plain yogurt or kefir
- 2 tablespoons rolled oats (optional, skip if very nauseous)
- 3/4 cup cold water or coconut water
- 1 teaspoon honey (optional)
- A few ice cubes

**How to make it:** add the liquid first, then everything else, and blend until completely smooth. Ginger fibers can be stringy, so blend a little longer than usual or strain if needed.

**Why it works:** the banana gives soft carbs and potassium without being heavy. Ginger has been studied as an anti-nausea remedy in pregnancy, motion sickness, and after surgery, with mixed but generally encouraging results. It hasn't been tested much on hangovers specifically, but it's a reasonable thing to try. Yogurt adds protein so you don't get a spike and crash from the fruit sugar.

**How to drink it:** take small sips over 20 to 30 minutes. Gulping a big cold drink on a sick stomach is a good way to bring it straight back up. If even this feels like too much, start with a few sips of plain water or ginger tea and come back to it later. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more options for settling your stomach.

## Recipe 2: Coconut-Citrus Rehydrator (Best for Thirst)

This is for the mornings when your mouth is dry, your head is pounding, and you can't stop drinking water. It's light, fruity, and built around fluid.

**Ingredients (makes 1 large glass):**

- 1 cup coconut water
- 1/2 cup frozen pineapple or mango chunks
- 1/2 banana
- Juice of half a lime
- 2 to 3 tablespoons orange juice (optional)
- A small pinch of salt (about 1/16 teaspoon)
- Ice to taste

**How to make it:** blend everything until smooth. Taste it. It should taste fruity with no obvious saltiness. If it tastes salty, you've added too much.

**Why it works:** coconut water is mostly water with a fair amount of potassium, but it's naturally low in sodium. Sodium is what helps your body hold on to fluid rather than passing it straight through, which is why medical rehydration drinks contain it. A small pinch of salt closes that gap. The fruit adds sugar, which also helps your gut absorb sodium and water, and the lime makes it taste fresh rather than sweet.

**A note on salt:** a pinch is plenty. You don't need to turn a smoothie into a salty drink. If you have high blood pressure or have been told to limit sodium, leave it out and use a regular electrolyte drink only if your doctor is fine with that. For a more detailed look at fluids and electrolytes, see our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

## Recipe 3: Green Recovery Smoothie (Best When You're Wiped Out)

This one is for the slow, foggy, low-energy hangover where your stomach is fine but you feel drained. It has more substance, with greens, protein, and a bit of fat.

**Ingredients (makes 1 large glass):**

- 1 large handful of baby spinach
- 1 banana
- 1 kiwi, peeled (or 1/2 cup frozen mango)
- 1/2 cup plain Greek yogurt
- 1 tablespoon peanut or almond butter
- 3/4 cup milk or unsweetened plant milk
- A few ice cubes

**How to make it:** blend the spinach and milk first until there are no flecks of leaf, then add the rest and blend again. This gives a smoother texture.

**Why it works:** heavy drinking can lower levels of some nutrients over time, especially folate, thiamine (vitamin B1), and magnesium, in people who drink a lot regularly. One smoothie won't fix that, and for an occasional night out there's no good evidence that topping up vitamins changes how bad your hangover feels. But spinach brings folate and magnesium, the kiwi adds vitamin C, and the yogurt and nut butter add protein and fat that keep you full and steady through the morning. It's a solid breakfast that happens to work on a hangover day.

**Skip it if you're nauseous.** Fat and fiber slow down how fast your stomach empties, which is good when you're well and less good when you're queasy. Go back to Recipe 1 instead. If you're curious about supplements, our [vitamins for hangover guide](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) explains which ones have any evidence.

## Recipe 4: Berry Protein Smoothie (Best When You're Starving)

Some hangovers come with a big appetite and a craving for anything salty, greasy, or sweet. This smoothie is filling enough to take the edge off that craving and buys you time to make a proper meal.

**Ingredients (makes 1 large glass):**

- 1 cup frozen mixed berries
- 1/2 banana
- 3/4 cup plain Greek yogurt or kefir (or 1 scoop of a plain protein powder plus 1/2 cup water)
- 2 tablespoons rolled oats
- 1 tablespoon chia seeds or ground flaxseed (optional)
- 3/4 cup milk or water
- Honey to taste

**How to make it:** blend until smooth. If it's too thick, add more liquid a splash at a time. Chia seeds will thicken it further if it sits, so drink it soon or add extra liquid.

**Why it works:** this has the most protein of the five recipes, plus slow-digesting carbs from the oats. Together they keep blood sugar steadier than a fruit-only smoothie, and they keep you full for longer. Berries add vitamin C and fiber. You'll see berries described as anti-inflammatory "hangover fighters," but there's no good evidence that a cup of berries makes a measurable difference to hangover symptoms. They're in here because they taste good and make a solid meal.

**About protein powder:** if you use one, check the label. Some contain caffeine or other stimulants, which you probably don't want on a morning when your heart may already be beating faster than usual. Some also use large amounts of sugar alcohols (like sorbitol or erythritol), which can cause bloating and loose stools on a gut that's already irritated.

## Recipe 5: Watermelon-Mint Cooler (Best When You Feel Hot and Sticky)

Some hangovers come with a sweaty, overheated feeling, especially after a summer night out or a long day in the sun. This one is thin, icy, and almost all water.

**Ingredients (makes 1 large glass):**

- 2 cups cubed seedless watermelon
- Juice of half a lime
- 5 or 6 fresh mint leaves
- A small pinch of salt
- 1/2 cup ice (or freeze the watermelon cubes ahead of time)
- 1/2 cup plain yogurt (optional, for a creamier, more filling version)

**How to make it:** blend everything until smooth. Strain it if you want a juice texture instead of a smoothie.

**Why it works:** watermelon is roughly 90 percent water, so this is about as hydrating as a smoothie gets. Mint is refreshing and some people find it soothing on the stomach (though if you have heartburn, mint can make reflux worse, so leave it out). You'll sometimes see watermelon promoted for an amino acid it contains called citrulline. There's no good evidence that citrulline does anything meaningful for a hangover, so think of this as a tasty way to drink more water, not a remedy.

**Make it more filling:** on its own this is low in protein and calories. If you're hungry, add the yogurt, or eat something alongside it, such as toast or eggs. Our [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) guide has ideas.

## Hangover Smoothie for Nausea: What to Change

If your stomach is the main problem, a few tweaks make any of these recipes easier to keep down:

- **Keep it small.** Make half a glass. You can always make more.
- **Keep it simple.** Three or four ingredients is plenty. Banana, ginger, and water or coconut water is enough.
- **Go easy on fat.** Nut butter, avocado, and full-fat milk slow stomach emptying. Save them for when you feel better.
- **Limit raw greens and seeds.** Large amounts of fiber can be harder to handle on a sore gut.
- **Avoid big splashes of acidic juice.** Orange, grapefruit, and pineapple juice can sting an irritated stomach.
- **Cold is usually better than warm.** Many people find cold drinks easier to tolerate when they feel sick.
- **Sip, don't gulp.** A few sips every couple of minutes is the way to go.

If you've vomited, wait until you've been able to hold down small sips of water for 15 to 30 minutes before trying a smoothie.

## Hangover Smoothie Before Bed or the Night Before

A good trick is to prepare your smoothie before you go out, so it's waiting for you in the morning.

- **Make it ahead.** Blend it, pour it into a sealed jar, and refrigerate. Most smoothies keep well for about a day. They may separate or darken a little, so shake before drinking.
- **Or make a freezer pack.** Put the fruit, greens, oats, and ginger into a freezer bag. In the morning, tip it into the blender with your liquid and blend.
- **Drink one before you go out.** A smoothie with protein and some fat (for example, Recipe 3 or Recipe 4) is a reasonable pre-drinking snack. Drinking on a full stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream compared with drinking on an empty one. It won't stop you getting drunk, and it won't prevent a hangover if you drink a lot, but it helps. See our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) for the habits with the best evidence.

Drinking a whole smoothie in bed right after a night out is less useful. A big glass of water before you sleep is simpler and more helpful, and your stomach may not thank you for a large cold meal at 2 a.m.

## Ingredients to Skip or Use With Care

Not everything that sounds healthy is a good idea on a hangover morning.

- **Alcohol.** Adding a shot to your smoothie (the "hair of the dog") only delays the hangover. It doesn't fix it.
- **Raw eggs.** Some old-school recovery shakes use raw egg for protein. Raw eggs carry a small risk of salmonella. Use yogurt, milk, or pasteurized egg products instead.
- **Strong caffeine.** Adding cold brew or espresso can help with grogginess for some people, but caffeine can also worsen anxiety, jitters, and a racing heart. If you normally drink coffee, a regular cup is fine. Don't stack it with energy drinks or caffeinated protein powders.
- **Grapefruit.** Grapefruit and grapefruit juice interact with a number of prescription medicines, including some blood pressure and cholesterol drugs. If you take regular medicine, check with a pharmacist before using it.
- **"Detox" powders and herbal blends.** These often have little evidence behind them, and some herbs can interact with medicines. If you're not sure what something does, leave it out.
- **Lots of added sugar.** Several tablespoons of honey, syrup, or sweetened yogurt can give you a quick lift and then a slump. A teaspoon or two is fine.

**If you have diabetes,** be careful with fruit-heavy smoothies, juice, and honey. Alcohol already makes blood sugar less predictable for the next day or so. Use more protein and less fruit, and follow the advice your care team has given you about drinking.

## Common Mistakes With Hangover Smoothies

- **Treating the smoothie as your only fluid.** A single glass is roughly 300 to 450 ml (10 to 15 ounces). Keep drinking water through the day as well.
- **Making it too big.** A giant blender jug of smoothie on a sore stomach is a recipe for regret.
- **Making it all fruit.** A fruit-only blend is basically juice with fiber. Add some protein so you're not hungry and shaky an hour later.
- **Chasing a "cure" ingredient.** Spirulina, activated charcoal, and so-called detox greens get a lot of attention online. There is no good evidence that any of them improves a hangover, and activated charcoal can interfere with how you absorb some medicines.
- **Ignoring warning signs.** A smoothie is for the normal, miserable kind of hangover. It isn't a treatment for severe vomiting, confusion, or chest symptoms.

## When a Hangover Is Something More

Most hangovers are unpleasant but harmless, and they're gone by the evening. But a few signals mean you should stop treating it at home:

- **You can't keep fluids down** for several hours, or you keep vomiting.
- **You see blood** in vomit or it looks like coffee grounds, or your stools are black.
- **You have severe or worsening stomach pain**, especially pain that spreads to your back.
- **Your heart is racing, pounding, or irregular**, or you have chest pain or shortness of breath.
- **You're confused, very drowsy, or fainting.**
- **The symptoms are getting worse after a day** instead of easing off.

If you drink heavily most days and notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, or seeing and hearing things when you cut back, that may be alcohol withdrawal. It can become dangerous, so talk to a doctor rather than trying to ride it out. And if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or has a seizure after drinking, call emergency services right away.

## Where DHM Fits In

Smoothies help with the morning after. They don't change how your body processes the alcohol in the first place. If you regularly wake up needing a recovery plan, some people also try supplements taken while or after drinking.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data, so it's promising but not settled. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright, and it doesn't replace drinking less, eating, and staying hydrated. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take regular medication, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- A hangover smoothie is a practical way to get fluids, calories, potassium, and protein into you when a real meal feels impossible. It is not a cure.
- **Feeling sick?** Make the banana-ginger smoothie, keep it small, and sip slowly.
- **Very thirsty?** Make the coconut-citrus rehydrator with a small pinch of salt.
- **Drained?** The green smoothie with yogurt and nut butter is a solid breakfast.
- **Starving?** The berry protein smoothie fills you up.
- **Hot and sticky?** The watermelon-mint cooler is mostly water.
- Keep drinking water through the day, skip raw eggs, extra alcohol, and "detox" powders, and get medical help if you can't keep fluids down or have any of the warning signs above.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best smoothie for a hangover?**

A good hangover smoothie combines fluid, a little sodium and potassium, some easy carbohydrates, and a bit of protein, and stays gentle on the stomach. A banana-ginger smoothie made with oats, yogurt, and water is a strong all-round choice, especially if you feel queasy. If your main problem is thirst, a coconut water and fruit smoothie with a pinch of salt is better. No smoothie cures a hangover, but the right one helps you get fluids and calories down when food sounds awful.

**Do hangover smoothies actually work?**

They help with some of the things that make a hangover worse, not with the hangover itself. A smoothie can get water, calories, potassium, and some sodium into you at a time when eating a full meal is hard, and ginger can ease nausea for some people. There is no good evidence that any smoothie ingredient speeds up how your body clears alcohol or its by-products. Time, rest, fluids, and food are still the main treatment.

**What should I put in a smoothie when I'm hungover and nauseous?**

Keep it small, cold, and simple: banana, fresh ginger, a few spoonfuls of plain yogurt or a handful of oats, and water or coconut water. Skip large amounts of fat (nut butter, avocado, full-fat milk), lots of raw greens, and very acidic juices, which can sit badly on an upset stomach. Sip slowly over 20 to 30 minutes rather than drinking it all at once. If you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, that needs medical attention.

**Is a smoothie better than a sports drink for a hangover?**

They do different jobs. A sports drink or oral rehydration solution gives a measured amount of sodium and sugar for rehydration, while a smoothie adds fiber, potassium, protein, and more calories. Most smoothies are low in sodium, so adding a small pinch of salt brings them closer to a rehydration drink. If you're mainly dehydrated, an electrolyte drink is the simpler choice. If you're also hungry but struggling to eat, a smoothie covers more ground.

**Can I make a hangover smoothie the night before?**

Yes. Blend it before you go out, pour it into a sealed jar, and keep it in the fridge. Most fruit smoothies keep well for about a day, though they can separate and the color can darken, so shake or stir before drinking. Another option is to pack the dry and frozen ingredients into a bag in the freezer so you only have to add liquid and blend in the morning.

**Should I add protein powder to a hangover smoothie?**

You can, if your stomach is up for it. Protein helps keep you full and steadies the meal, but plain Greek yogurt, kefir, milk, or a spoon of nut butter do the same job for most people. Check the label on any protein powder, since some contain caffeine, stimulants, or large doses of sugar alcohols that can upset an already irritated gut.

**Is it OK to drink a smoothie before drinking alcohol?**

Yes, and it's a reasonable idea. Drinking on a full stomach slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream compared with drinking on an empty one. A smoothie with protein, some fat, and fiber (for example yogurt, oats, banana, and a spoon of nut butter) works better for this than a thin fruit-only blend. It won't stop you from getting drunk or prevent a hangover if you drink a lot, but it helps you pace.
